articles.headline: Rockstar workers in the UK will hold a union vote just as GTA 6 is released
keyFacts: Rockstar workers in the UK are scheduled to vote on recognizing their union branch from November 12 to November 26, according to journalist Jason Schreier.
An employment tribunal concerning a union-busting complaint brought by the IWUGB against Rockstar is expected to conclude on November 17 or 18.
The union complaint followed the October 2025 layoffs of over 30 employees, whom Rockstar stated were let go due to misconduct involving confidential information.
body: Rockstar workers in the UK will hold a union vote just as GTA 6 is released
A legal case alleging union-busting at the game developer will also wrap next month.

Most gamers may be focused on the countdown to the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19, but there will also be a fair bit of drama unfolding behind the scenes at developer Rockstar Games over the coming weeks. According to a social media post from Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, workers at Rockstar's UK offices are reportedly scheduled to vote on recognizing their branch of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWUGB) from November 12 to November 26. If the employee vote is a success, the Rockstar Game Workers Union would become the largest recognized union in the UK's game industry.

Adding another layer to the combined cultural and corporate hype around late November, an employment tribunal between Rockstar and the IWUGB that was scheduled to end earlier in October has also been extended. That case is now expected to have closing arguments delivered on November 17 or 18, just before the GTA 6 launch. The IWUGB brought a complaint against Rockstar after the game developer laid off more than 30 employees in October 2025, most of whom were either union members or engaged in organizing efforts. The move raised alarms that the studio was engaged in union-busting, although the company claimed the employees were let go due to misconduct related to sharing confidential information. The Rockstar Game Workers Union, covering people at all of the company's offices across the UK, was announced in May 2026.

In a feature piece earlier this month that interviewed several people from Rockstar, Schreier reported that the unionizing workers who remained have been in ongoing discussion with the company's management in the intervening months. "We go where the team goes," Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar, told Schreier. "So if they want a union, they will have a union."

articles.headline: Apple Creator Studio Brings MotionVFX and AI Assistants to Subscribers
keyFacts: Apple announced AI-powered updates and new features for its Apple Creator Studio software suite on Tuesday.
The updates include MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro, an AI assistant for Logic Pro, and generative fill for Pixelmator Pro.
The updated software will be available as a free update for existing subscribers in November.
body: Apple really is “Pro and Tell“-ing us a lot of news this week. On Tuesday, the company announced that its suite of creative software, Apple Creator Studio, will receive a bevy of AI-powered updates. That’s in addition to the new iMac, MacBook Pros and new OLED iPad Mini that the company also announced this week.

Final Cut Pro, Apple’s professional-grade video editor, is getting built-in MotionVFX. That should bring more visual and graphic effects tools to content editors on Mac. Logic Pro is getting a new beta AI assistant (powered by AI models built by Apple and OpenAI) for music editors in the US, along with a redesigned browser that uses Apple’s new Liquid Glass aesthetic. Pixelmator Pro is getting a kind of generative fill tool that uses AI to resize and fill in the gaps in new images; it sounds like it may be similar to Photoshop’s popular generative fill.

In Apple’s business software, expect to see new AI assistants in Keynote, Pages and Numbers. These are likely similar to how Google has integrated Gemini into its software over the past few years (and hopefully less annoying). The updated software will be available as “a free update for existing subscribers” in November.
More from CNET

The Apple news has been fast and furious this fall. The Cupertino-based company dropped the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. Then it refreshed its entire smart home lineup, complete with a new HomeView device. We’re expecting even more Apple hardware news to drop on Wednesday, the in-person day of its Pro and Tell event that experts say could bring another long-awaited Apple first: a touchscreen MacBook. CNET is tracking all the Apple shenanigans this week and testing the new iPhone Duo — by folding it over 75,000 times and counting.

You can buy individual, lifetime (or “universal” as Apple calls it) subscriptions to each of Apple’s creative software. But these new features are coming only to Apple Creator Studio subscribers, who have access to multiple programs and pay a higher price tag as a result. Apple Creator Studio subscriptions start at $13 per month, and if you do buy a new MacBook, you get a free three-month trial.

articles.headline: Former Halo boss is now in charge of Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games
keyFacts: Dan Ayoub has been promoted to head Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games, succeeding John Hight.
Ayoub will oversee major projects including the sci-fi RPG Exodus and the third-person action-adventure Warlock: Dungeons and Dragons.
Hasbro stated that Ayoub was chosen after a search evaluating dozens of internal and external candidates.
body: Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games have a new boss, and it's kind of the old boss. Dan Ayoub, who spent the past couple years as senior vice president of digital games at Wizards, has been promoted to the big chair, where he'll head up Magic: The Gathering, Dungeons and Dragons, Duel Masters, and Hasbro Digital Games.

Ayoub will take the place of John Hight, who left the position in July after just two years on the job. On the videogame-specific side of things, Ayoub will now oversee two major projects in development: The Mass Effect-like sci-fi RPG Exodus being developed by Archetype Entertainment, and the third-person action-adventure Warlock: Dungeons and Dragons, being made by Invoke Studios.
"[Ayoub] was selected after a rigorous search that evaluated dozens of internal and external candidates," Hasbro said. "He is the first internal candidate promoted into the role."

Ayoub has real experience in the biz: Prior to joining Wizards of the Coast, he served as executive producer and studio head at Halo studio 343 Industries, and also spent more than a year as vice president and general manager of co-development studio Certain Affinity.

"I'm honored to lead Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games, and grateful to Chris [Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks] and the leadership team for this opportunity," Ayoub said. "Magic and D&D have been part of my life for as long as I can remember, and the teams behind them are among the best in the world. We'll put fans first, respect the artists and creators who make these worlds come alive, and set an ambitious course for growth across tabletop and digital. I can't wait to get started."

But he also comes into the new role at a challenging time. Despite going hard on videogames in the immediate aftermath of Baldur's Gate 3, Hasbro has struggled to actually follow up on it: The company recorded a $56 million non-cash impairment earlier this year arising from the cancellation of several games in development that were expected to release "in 2028 and beyond."

Potentially complicating matters further, Cocks, the Hasbro CEO, is a vocal AI enthusiast. He recently indicated that he wasn't pushing to incorporate it in Hasbro games because people "just don't want it," he was also clear that he views widespread generative AI use as the inevitable future: "You can't ignore it, you can't stick your head in the sand." In that light, Ayoub's remark about respecting "artists and creators" might be seen as a little more meaningful—but how that holds up in the long run, we will have to wait and see.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.headline: Vance tears into ‘psychopath’ Abdul El-Sayed, blasts Dem for peddling ‘anti-white’ hatred
keyFacts: Vice President JD Vance criticized Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as an extremist during a campaign visit to Michigan.
Vance campaigned for Republican Mike Rogers while polls showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 2.5 percentage points.
Vance claimed El-Sayed promotes anti-white hatred and lied about his background, but provided no additional details.
body: HOWELL, Mich. — Vice President JD Vance ripped Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed as a “psychopath” during a trip to Michigan Tuesday — claiming that the lefty candidate was “ashamed” of the state, is pushing “anti-white racial hatred,” and will likely kill off the local auto industry.

Vance used his high-profile visit to make a last-ditch pitch to swing voters that El-Sayed was an unacceptable radical — as polls show him virtually tied with or leading Republican Mike Rogers one week from Election Day.

“Abdul El Sayed is a little bit of a psychopath, and we’re going to just try to make the argument as well as we can and help Mike out a little bit,” Vance said before boarding Air Force Two en route to a rally attended by several hundred people outside Detroit.

El-Sayed has “engaged in the kind of explicitly anti-white racial hatred” perhaps “more than any Democrat running in the nation,” the veep boomed, calling the candidate “a guy who seems to love to traffic in racial hatred.”
Vance did not provide additional detail on his allegation that El-Sayed was a racist.
When he arrived in Michigan, Vance told a cheering crowd that El-Sayed was an extremist.
If recent rioting in France spread to Detroit, El-Sayed would be “right there and cheering them on,” he said.

“Abdul El-Sayed was born just north of Detroit in a town called Rochester Hills. Yet he is claiming to be, and I quote, ‘an immigrant from North Africa.’ For decades, he’s gone even further than that. He told people he is an Egyptian citizen,” the VP said.

“Why? Why would you tell people that you were not from the community that you’re actually from? It’s an insane claim to make… [He is] a man who would lie, who is so ashamed of this state that he would lie about being an immigrant from another continent.”

Vance added that El-Sayed “says that he wants to pass the green new scam and kill the auto industry of this state” and has “campaigned with his best friend Hassan Piker, a man who said that we deserved 9/11.”
The broadsides come as El-Sayed leads Rogers by 2.5 percentage points, according to the RealClearPolitics average of recent polls.

Vance brushed off former Fox News host Tucker Carlson’s vehement opposition to Rogers, a hawkish former chairman of the House intelligence committee, calling the Republican “fundamentally a decent guy and the kind of public servant that you want in Washington, D.C.”

He also stopped short of embracing President Trump’s characterization of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, as a “jihadist,” saying instead, “I don’t know what’s in the guy’s heart. I just know he has a lot of weird friends.”
El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

articles.headline: Google's Android Registered App Stores program launches Dec. 1, applications now open
keyFacts: Google opened applications for its Registered App Stores program, which launches globally outside the US on December 1.
Approved third-party app stores will receive preferential platform treatment, including single-click installations and silent background updates.
Google stated the program aims to provide third-party stores a streamlined reach while maintaining ecosystem safety and security.
body: Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program. Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.

App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.

“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”

The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.

Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.

articles.headline: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
keyFacts: Elon Musk claimed Ukraine's military violated Starlink terms of service by using the satellite internet for offensive drone strikes.
Ukrainian officials denied the allegations, stating that commercial Starlink terminals lack the technical capability to function on fast-moving drones.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield services were fully restored, allowing connections at speeds over 400 kilometers per hour.
body: Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica. According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do.
Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
Musk accuses Ukraine’s military of using Starlink to carry out drone strikes, which officials have denied.

The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios, Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink.

Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote.

Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400kmh (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports.

Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

articles.headline: 175 Democrats demand Trump admin stop Ilhan Omar investigation, warn it could hurt her re-election bid
keyFacts: Nearly 200 House Democrats demanded the Trump administration halt its investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar, calling the probe a partisan attack meant to sway her re-election bid.
Federal investigators are probing Omar's immigration history and previously raided her Washington, D.C., home regarding paperwork filed by her late father.
Democrats argued in their letter that the investigation violates policies against taking investigative steps close to an election.
body: Nearly 200 House Democrats are moving to shield Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., from further investigation after federal investigators raided her Washington, D.C., home earlier this month.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal , D-Wash., led 175 members of the House Democratic Caucus in a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche, criticizing the probe into Omar's immigration history as a partisan attack and accusing them of trying to sway her bid for another term in Congress.

"Congresswoman Omar is seeking reelection in Minnesota’s 5th congressional district in just one week. News of the search warrant, whether properly predicated or not, could affect voters’ decisions, which is exactly why federal law enforcement should not engage in such conduct when voters are casting their ballots. This type of interference strips Minnesotans of their right to a free and fair election guaranteed to them under the Constitution," the letter said.

"We stand with Congresswoman Omar and condemn the weaponization of law enforcement against her. You have already disgraced the offices you hold, and we demand you refrain from taking any further actions that could affect the outcome of the upcoming election."
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’

Omar, D-Minn., is under federal investigation over allegations she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. If she was 17 when her father obtained citizenship, as previously thought, she would have automatically qualified along with him. If she was 18 or older, which federal officials now suspect, she would have had to make her own application.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Her fellow House Democrats recounted the allegations in their letter, saying, "Your probe into the congresswoman reportedly concerns her late father’s filing of immigration paperwork after she fled Somalia’s civil war at age eight, making her a U.S. citizen at age seventeen."
But they argued it does not justify "a pre-dawn raid on her home for paperwork her father filed when she was a minor."
DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS
Federal agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant on Omar's home on Oct. 12, seizing multiple phones and notebooks, among other items.
"This weaponization of law enforcement to harass a sitting Member of Congress 22 days before an election is unprecedented and unacceptable," Democrats' letter said.

"DOJ has long followed a policy not to take investigative steps relating to a candidate this close to an election if delaying the action will not jeopardize a criminal investigation, a policy which Attorney General Blanche has previously invoked as far back as nine months before an election."
ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING
They argued the probe was "driven by a pre-determined political outcome rather than an objective pursuit of justice."
Omar has dismissed the probe as a political hit job against one of Trump's loudest critics.
Others, however, like House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., have called for Omar to be jailed and deported if the accusations are proven true.
Fox News Digital reached out to DHS and the Department of Justice for comment.

articles.headline: Why this new Fitbit feature takes us one step closer to non-invasive glucose tracking
keyFacts: Google added insulin resistance and blood pressure trend tracking to Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge devices for Google Health Premium subscribers.
The new features use algorithms to analyze biometric data and monitor metabolic health trends without direct skin penetration.
Eligible users who wear their devices for five days or more will receive monthly health insights in the app's Health tab.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Insulin resistance and blood pressure trends are coming to the Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge.
- These new features are available for Google Health Premium users only.
- The news points at Google’s greater health mission in developing a continuous glucose monitor.

Google just added insulin resistance and blood pressure trends to the Fitbit Air and Edge, taking these devices beyond basic fitness monitoring and sleep tracking and into deeper health insights. The new features are part of Google’s “Health Guardian” suite of proactive safety tools for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit.

They’re available solely for Google Health Premium users, a $100 annual subscription that grants users access to Google’s AI health coach, advanced sleep tracking, and a more expansive selection of health-tracking features.
More from ZDNET

While it doesn’t measure your insulin or glucose outright, its algorithm analyzes heart rate, activity level, sleep, and other metrics to show changes in metabolic health. The Fitbit will also track your blood pressure patterns without a cuff, monitor your pulse while you’re asleep or awake, and, at the end of the month, provide you with insights. Eligible Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge users who have worn their device for five days or more will see this insight in the Health tab of the app.

Similar to blood pressure trends, the insulin resistance feature uses Fitbit sensors to monitor shifts in metabolic health. Insulin resistance is a precursor to type 2 diabetes, potentially giving users insight into changes in their insulin levels in a less invasive way, but pointing more toward overall trends than a direct diagnosis.

Unlike a continuous glucose monitor, which penetrates the skin and uses blood to gather metabolic data, the insulin resistance feature was built to assess biometric and metabolic patterns through its multimodal model. Google trained its insulin resistance model on data gathered by other wearables as well as compiled demographic data, according to its paper in Nature.

Once the feature detects elevated insulin resistance patterns, it notifies the user to take additional action. Fitbit users can even connect their Abbott CGM to the Google Health app for additional glucose monitoring. By offering these Health Guardian features to more devices than just its flagship Pixel Watches, Google is giving more users — specifically budget-conscious users who own a $100 and $180 Fitbit Air or Edge — the ability to track and stay ahead of some common and serious health conditions.

While the insulin resistance feature is nowhere near the capabilities of a non-invasive CGM, Google’s development of a multimodal model for tracking biometric responses to insulin activity suggests the company is getting closer to that non-invasive reality.

Non-invasive glucose monitoring is like the foldable phone of wearable technology. It’s a product idea that’s been around for years now, and every tech company is racing to deploy its own, with varying degrees of success and adoption. Even Steve Jobs had dreams of an Apple glucose monitor that people could use — no finger prick necessary. Rumors suggest that Apple has also been working on this for years now.

But Google might be a few steps ahead of Apple on this one. Its deployment of insulin resistance trends to new Fitbit devices is one way it is advancing toward a CGM that uses algorithmic AI instead of needles and blood.

articles.headline: Lupin: Part 4 Review
keyFacts: Lupin: Part 4 is streaming on Netflix, featuring an eight-episode season that soft-reboots the French heist series with soap opera melodrama.
IGN stated that the new season follows gentleman thief Assane Diop as he faces new heists, family tensions with his son Raoul, and a complex conspiracy.
IGN reported that the season ends in an unexpected place, setting up potential dilemmas for a possible fifth season.
body: Lupin: Part 4 is on Netflix now.

It’s been three years since Lupin’s last season — a less memorable, less focused entry — so you’d be forgiven for forgetting much of what transpired. The show’s fourth part features an extended recap narrated by the title character before kicking off in earnest, at which point it hits the “soft reboot” button, both narratively and stylistically. Its biggest change is a welcome one: it leans unapologetically into the soap opera underpinnings which have always made it tick. The result is a brisk eight episodes that, despite wheel-spinning near the season’s end, eventually find their way to the kind of ludicrous melodrama that makes the French heist series such a turn-your-brain-off delight.

Part 3 ended with a major cliffhanger, as gentleman thief Assane Diop (Omar Sy) — a devotee of Maurice Leblanc’s fictitious fraudster Arsène Lupin — found himself in prison, in a cell adjacent to his long time, opulent enemy Hubert Pellegrini (Hervé Pierre). How does the new season resolve this tension? Well, it doesn’t. Which is to say, it treats the whole thing like a gag in order for the show to move forward into unexpected territory. Four years have passed, and in that time, Assane has willingly remained behind bars — except for a brief escape where he bamboozled Pellegrini all the way into a shipping container bound for a Malaysian prison. Now on the verge of release for good behavior, it finally seems like Assane has turned over a new leaf. That is, until a slickly-executed pair of simultaneous heists, in his signature style, make the police suspicious, forcing him to go rogue in order to prove his innocence.

During Assane’s prison stint, his teenage son Raoul (now played by newcomer Théo Christine) has grown into a frustrated young adult in want of an absent father. Once a mere plot device and kidnapping victim, Raoul now becomes the series’ unexpected heart and soul, though the narrative, and Assane, keep shoving him to the side until those frustrations reach a boiling point. A winding conspiracy takes precedence, involving a copycat swindler and twists and turns ripped right from a daytime soap opera — a secret lineage, sudden deaths, equally sudden resurrections, and so on — forcing Lupin to unexpectedly turn to former foes for new partnerships in search of a secret treasure. All the while, his police frenemy Youssef Guédira (Soufiane Guerrab), a fellow Leblanc enthusiast, remains on his tail, but is less willing to offer him the benefit of doubt when his partner Sofia Belkacem (Shirine Boutella) is gravely injured.

It's a brisk eight episodes that, despite wheel-spinning near season’s end, eventually find their way to the kind of ludicrous melodrama that makes the series such a turn-your-brain-off delight. Complicating matters further is the fact that, in Assane’s absence, his best friend and co-conman Benjamin (Antoine Gouy) has fallen for his ex-wife and Raoul’s mother, Claire (Ludivine Sagnier), adding yet another layer to the sprawling flashbacks of the various characters as teens and young adults. Was this pairing always in the cards? Of course not, but the fourth season also goes a long way towards re-writing the show’s basic DNA. These flashbacks involve both interpersonal drama and a surprising amount of setup for the contemporary conspiracies, as though the central plot of this season — involving a secret society with some icky blood-purity leanings, playing into the show’s modern, pluralistic re-imagining of Leblanc’s Lupin — had been decades in the making. Like Assane himself, the show is a bullshit artist of the highest caliber; it works to convince you that every twisting screw is part of some intricately devised puzzle dating back to its 2021 debut, when it’s all clearly been designed on-the-fly.

And yet, that design yields some clockwork thrills from time to time, between Assane’s continued weaponization of racial prejudice to pull off his galaxy-brained heists (one scheme in particular involves a flashmob of re-enactors dressed as an oft-forgotten Black French general) and the style with which the series presents each deceit. The editing is more judicious this time. To reveal how a given ploy was pulled off, it relies less on unseen angles and elements when episodes re-visit existing scenes, and more on parts of the image you might’ve missed in the first place.

The season’s broader themes of family allow Lupin to become a particularly silly bit of business akin to the later Fast & Furious films. Assane becomes increasingly torn between making up for lost time with Raoul and tracking down lost jewels with a newly-formed family of thieves who start out the season at odds. Among these is a mixed-race character named Adèle Kapoor (Laïka Blanc-Francard) who, in addition to expanding the show’s quickfire (if malformed) invocations of racism in modern France, becomes the center of a tech-infused update to the series with her skills as a hacker in the age of A.I. deepfakes. The less said about her backstory beforehand, the better, but that she’s on par with Assane as a Leblanc-inspired burglar and gives him a much-needed rival and dramatic counterweight.

The show’s new directions aren’t necessarily original — here you’ll find familiar gadgets, scenes and dynamics straight out of everything from Bond, Indiana Jones and Mission: Impossible to the network procedural White Collar — but Lupin’s fourth part sublimates all these influences into something cheekily enjoyable. It rides a fine line between heightened, crisscrossing nonsense plots and intensified character-centric schmaltz, but when it counts the most, it manages to find just the right balance between the two, before leaving off in perhaps the most unexpected place this series could go. If there is a fifth season (and there really should be), the dilemmas facing Assane will probably make for damn good television, given the various pieces Part 4 moves gradually into place.

articles.headline: UK-based Rockstar devs will be putting their union recognition to a vote during GTA 6's launch next month
keyFacts: Rockstar Games staff will vote on union recognition from November 12 to November 26, according to the Independent Workers of Great Britain.
The union stated a successful vote would give workers a say over pay, bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working, and generative AI policies.
Closing arguments for an employment tribunal regarding alleged union busting will occur between November 17 and November 18.
body: November is potentially going to be big for Rockstar Games, and not just because of that GTA 6 thing they're doing. As shared in a press release from the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB), recognition of the IWGB Union at Rockstar will be voted upon by staffers at the studio, with votes being held from November 12th (a week before GTA 6's launch date) and November 26th.

"The terms of the recognition deal, agreed upon by workers and management, would give workers a say over topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies," the press release explains. It also notes that if the vote is successful, the union will become the largest recognised union in the UK games industry.

This also comes at another pivotal time for Rockstar workers, both current and former alike. Almost exactly a year ago, Rockstar laid off 31 staffers in an alleged act of union busting. Fast forward to now, and an employment tribunal is being held between the game developer, the IWGB, and the laid off workers. Closing arguments for the tribunal will take place between November 17th and 18th, mere days ahead of the game's launch. It'll still be a while until a judge decides if Rockstar did break employment law.

In a statement, Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said, "For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them. When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."
Solidarity with the workers as always. GTA 6 will undoubtedly be the biggest game of the decade, and everyone that has worked on it deserves to be properly compensated and assuaged of their concerns.

- Rockstar are "confident" that GTA 7 won't take another eight years, despite similar promises of greater efficiency seemingly having come with Red Dead Redemption 2
- GTA 6 PC release planned for early 2027, report claims, which could mean we're playing in time for GTA Online 2: Vice City 4 U or whatever they call it

articles.headline: EU privacy advocates accuse US data annotation firm of snooping on contractors
keyFacts: Privacy campaigner noyb filed five GDPR complaints in four EU countries accusing US data annotation firm Scale AI of unlawfully monitoring European contractors.
Noyb alleged that Scale and verification provider Persona collect biometric data, track device activity, and transmit information to third parties like LinkedIn and TikTok.
Scale denied the allegations, stating that its practices are disclosed, require consent, and are used for identity verification and fraud prevention.
body: US data annotation operation Scale AI faces five GDPR complaints in four EU countries over allegations that it unlawfully monitors European contractors.

Privacy campaigner noyb alleges that Scale tracks contractors who perform data annotation work on its Outlier AI platform. Like workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform of yore, Outlier contractors label data, evaluate AI-generated responses, and perform other tasks to improve AI models. Scale counts companies including OpenAI, xAI, Anthropic, and Google, as well as the US government , among its customers.

Scale AI faces allegations similar to those noyb has made against other US tech firms since the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) went into effect in 2018, namely violations of said regulation.
With all that work being done digitally and remotely, Scale has extensive data collection practices to not only verify the identity of Outlier workers, but also to extensively track their activity.

“Platform work seems to be fertile ground for a whole new type of workplace surveillance,” said Thomas Le Bonniec, sociology researcher at French privacy research group DIPLab, who co-authored a report earlier this month examining Outlier's data collection practices. “This would be seen as unacceptable in any other form of employment in the European Union.”

Among the issues that raised the hackles of noyb's lawyers was identity verification conducted by Persona, a company that has faced scrutiny over an exposed test environment associated with its efforts to secure US government business. Researchers speculated that the system could be used to build a people tracker, but Persona rejected that interpretation and denied having active US government contracts. Separately, Persona's relationship with chat app Discord soured ahead of the platform's broader age verification rollout, with Discord saying the provider failed to meet its requirements for on-device facial age estimation.

According to noyb, Persona collects biometric data to verify Outlier contractors are who they say they are, as well as gathering IP addresses, device info, geolocation data, addresses, and credit data of Outlier users.

In addition to the biometric identification data, noyb accuses Scale of tracking Outlier workers by collecting system data and device activity (including activity outside of Outlier work), and transmitting that to third parties including LinkedIn, TikTok, Facebook, and other analytics services as often as every few seconds. Noyb warns that the information could be used to profile individuals and serve targeted advertising.

“Such constant and extensive tracking while working really goes against all reasonable expectations,” noyb data protection lawyer Lisa Steinfeld Leiser said of the allegations. “Why should LinkedIn or Facebook know which tasks you're working on?”

Noyb has filed complaints in France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Austria against Scale, arguing that it lacks a legal basis to install tracking software on contractors’ devices. The US company also stands accused of violating GDPR rules on data minimization, which requires that companies only collect data that’s strictly necessary for specific purposes. The complaints also assert Scale violated GDPR rights to data access after ignoring complainants’ requests to access the records of what data Scale had stored on them, as well as country-specific laws in the nations where the complaints were filed.
Noyb is asking data protection authorities in those nations to conduct a full investigation and, if necessary, fine Scale for its alleged violations.

""The report’s claims are unfounded and inaccurate," Scale told us after this article was first published. "Outlier’s practices are disclosed to contributors and require their consent. We use standard tools to verify identities, prevent fraud, protect confidential project information, and ensure accurate payment."

The complaint is likely to give further fuel to the digital sovereignty movement sweeping the EU, which has begun to realize in the past couple of years that it may not be in the best interest of the bloc to be entirely beholden to US tech companies, even if such a separation may be painfully difficult . ®
Updated at 1730 UTC to include comment from Scale.

articles.headline: 8-month Iran war looms large over Israeli election
keyFacts: Israelis voted in a national election on Tuesday while their defense minister urged voters to back Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to finish the war in Iran.
A Kuwaiti court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged assassination plot and accusations of spying for Iran and joining Hezbollah.
Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for a missile strike that caused massive fires at the Ras Tanura oil refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia.
body: What to know about the Iran war:

- Israelis were voting Tuesday in a national, with the looming large over their decisions. Israel's defense minister called on voters to back Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration so it can "finish the job" started in Iran almost eight months ago.

- Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting.

- Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said Tuesday that Egypt's to Saudi Arabia to defend against the rebels' attacks on the kingdom was a "declaration of war," as the interwoven conflicts in the Middle East threatened to escalate.
Kuwait sentences 3 men to death over alleged assassination plot and links to Iran, Hezbollah

A Kuwaiti State Security and Terrorism Criminal Court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged plot to assassinate First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef, with prosecutors accusing the defendants of spying for Iran, communicating with Iranian-linked entities and joining Hezbollah, two judicial sources told the AFP news agency Tuesday.
The court also sentenced eight other defendants to varying prison terms.

Those sentenced to death included cleric and National Islamic Alliance Secretary-General Hussein Abdullah Al-Maatouq and two other men. One of the defendants had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received a pardon before being arrested again in April, the sources said.

According to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai, the defendants were accused of communicating with Iran and entities allegedly operating in its interests, including Lebanese group Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Feb. 28, at the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The defendants were also accused of joining Hezbollah, a banned group in Kuwait, while knowing its objectives, and of engaging in activities allegedly intended to undermine the country's political, social and economic order and harm its national interests.

Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Qabas reported prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the alleged assassination plot and spread panic. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.

The reported Iran connection forms a central part of the case, although the allegations against the defendants do not, on their own, establish that the Iranian government directed the alleged assassination plot.
Houthis claim missile strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed Tuesday to have struck a refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia.

"With the help of Almighty God, the Yemeni Armed Forces succeeded in targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a post on X.
"The strike was accurate," he added, "and caused massive fires at the targeted site."
The alleged strike follows weeks of Houthi attacks against the world's top exporter of crude oil.
A resident in the nearby city of Al Khobar told the AFP news agency he heard explosions around dawn and then received a warning message on his phone.
"We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang," the resident said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia's eastern Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and is a cornerstone of the kingdom's energy sector.

The complex has a capacity to refine 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by Iranian strikes, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.
CBS/AFP
U.K. charges 2 men arrested over alleged Iran-linked terror plot against RAF Fairford air base used by U.S.

London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a in England.
U.S. embassy in Baghdad shoots down two drones, according to Al-Arabiya
The U.S. embassy in Baghdad has shot down two drones, Saudi state television channel Al Arabya reported Tuesday.
An Iraqi security source told the outlet that air defenses protecting the embassy destroyed the drones.

The government-owned Iraqi television channel Al-Anbar reported that the head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, Saad Maan, said that explosions heard across the capital were the result of a drone being intercepted and shot down.
The drone's origin remains unknown, and no immediate reports of casualties or damage have been released. The U.S. State Department has not yet commented on the incident.
Experts warn of effects of slick as oil seen on UAE beach
An oil slick in the Gulf has reached a beach in the United Arab Emirates, video from the AFP news agency showed on Tuesday, with experts warning it could threaten desalination plants as it spreads.
UAE authorities said Friday that they had "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
By Tuesday morning, footage shot by AFP showed workers cleaning up oil on the emirate's beaches, which had been shut earlier by authorities along with other beaches in the country.

Satellite images taken on Oct. 21 and analyzed by AFP show what appears to be a slick of about 70 square miles in that area. Three days later, images showed it had quadrupled in size to around 290 square miles.
Experts from NGOs including Dutch peace group PAX said oil came from the tanker GEM NO.2 after it was attacked on Oct. 9.
They warned the slick could affect operations at UAE desalination plants, crucial for supplying water to the Gulf country.

"Satellite imagery from October 26 shows oil slicks a few hundred metres away from the intake of the Naqaa desalination plant. It remains unclear to what extent this will affect the process at the plant itself," said Wim Zwijnenburg from PAX.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
CBS/AFP
Iranian official says Middle Eastern countries must stop relying on the U.S. for security

Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said regional countries should not rely on the United States for security, arguing that Washington has failed to provide credible security guarantees.

In a post on X Tuesday, Rezaee wrote: "America has not brought security to any country in the region, and Washington's inability to provide security guarantees has become clear. Security in West Asia must originate from within the region, and any foreign intervention must be prevented."
The U.S. has military bases in several Gulf countries that repeatedly were targeted at the height of the war.
Houthi official calls Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia a declaration of war

A Houthi official said Tuesday that the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to help the kingdom defend against the Iran-backed group's attacks was a declaration of war.

"Egypt and its parliament declared support for what is called the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, it declares war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi political bureau, in a Telegram post.
El-Sisi that the Egyptian deployment would be entirely defensive, "and does not include an attack on Yemen."
CBS/AFP
Oil prices stick around $116 a barrel despite Iran lauding talks with Saudis and others aimed at averting new fighting

Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting. Tehran said the discussions were "very good."
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.

The talks followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, with some observers suggesting the period between next Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections and the new Congress taking office could be particularly fraught.
Also in view are elections in Israel, where voters began delivering their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who told President Trump a week ago that they have "a job to finish" in Iran.
CBS/AFP
As Israeli election begins, defense chief calls on voters to let Netanyahu "finish the job" in Iran
Israelis started casting votes Tuesday morning in a national , with the Iran war looming large over their decisions.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, echoing warnings issued repeatedly by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for weeks leading up to the vote, told voters that they were facing a decision "between two security paradigms: an approach based on offense, initiative, and decisive victory — or a return to a policy of containment and restraint."

"We have struck Iran twice and eliminated existential threats; we have expanded Israel's security perimeter in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza to protect Israeli communities; and we are currently strengthening and fortifying our eastern border and the Jordan Valley," he said, calling on Israeli voters to "support this path in order to finish the job."
Netanyahu has called for Israel and the U.S. to resume attacks on Iran, telling President Trump, who has endorsed him enthusiastically, last week, "we have a job to finish."

The Iranian regime has dismissed the importance of the Israeli election, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters Monday that the outcome will have no bearing on Iran's preparedness to face a resumption of hostilities, or to negotiate a deal to end the war based on its longstanding demands.
Saudi coalition says it intercepted 3 Houthi ballistic missiles
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Tuesday that it had shot down three missiles fired by the group toward the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
Iran's talks with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Middle East security were "very good," officials say
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good."

Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.
The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.

The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.

But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital were "very good," according to state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.

He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention," saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Kuwait sentences 3 to death for alleged plot to kill deputy prime minister, sources say
Kuwait condemned three men to death on Monday for plotting the assassination of the deputy prime minister, collaborating with Iran and joining Hezbollah, two judiciary sources told AFP.
The three men are all from the Shia Muslim community, which makes up around a third of Kuwait's population.
Huseein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, was among the three condemned by the criminal court, the sources said.
Another of the trio had been convicted in 2016 of terrorism before being pardoned by the country's emir. He was arrested again in April, the sources said.

The men are accused of undermining national interests, collaborating with Iran, planning the assassination of the deputy prime minister and interior minister, and membership of Hezbollah, which is classified as a terrorist group by Kuwait.
The court sentenced 11 other people connected to the case to five years of hard labor.
Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Gulf countries, including Kuwait, have arrested dozens of people with suspected ties to Iran.
Vessel on fire off Iraq coast, U.K. maritime monitor says
A vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq on Monday, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, citing multiple third-party reports.
The vessel was situated 63 nautical miles from Al-Faw, a coastal town located along the Gulf between Iran and Kuwait, the maritime monitor said.
"Crew status, damage assessment, and environment impact are unknown," wrote UKMTO of the incident, which it deemed "suspicious activity."
The agency reminded those transiting the area to do so with caution while authorities investigate what may have occurred.
Netanyahu, rivals trade criticisms over Iran amid tight Israeli election race
Wrapping up his re-election campaign on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that Israel could face potential annihilation by Iran if his political rivals prevailed over him.

Over the course of a neck-and-neck race, Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" against Tehran and painting his main challenger, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, as soft on Israel's sworn foe.

"I think this is a fateful moment for the future of the state, because we have enemies who want to annihilate us," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel 14 the day before Tuesday's vote, adding, "Gadi Eisenkot will not strike Iran."

Eisenkot has in turn accused the premier of playing politics with security on the election's eve and citing the Iran threat when it suits him — an allegation that came after a report, citing unnamed sources, said there were concerns within the Israeli army that the war was being politicized.
Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish," and Defense Minister Israel Katz said any reports of a gap between the army and political leadership were "entirely baseless and false."
CBS/AFP
Delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey meet in Iran to try to avert renewed fighting

High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said. Iran and the three countries party to the Mecca defense pact — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — agreed to continue talks after a "first" meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the Monday meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security," while Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability."

Two regional officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters, told the Associated Press that the war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also among the topics discussed during the talks.

During the talks on Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries.

The meeting followed Qatari mediators' trip to Tehran on Sunday, which was coordinated alongside the U.S. and came as part of an effort to scale back regional tensions, a regional official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks, told AP.
AP/AFP
Putin to meet Iranian president and Qatari emir on sidelines of Moscow energy summit

Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold five bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, according to Interfax.

Pezeshkian said before departing Tehran that his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity in the Middle East, which he said was caused by the war sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran almost eight months ago.
Saudi-led coalition says three more drones shot down over Riyadh

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government in the escalating civil war with the Iran-backed Houthis claimed Monday to have shot down three more drones over the Saudi capital Riyadh, and in the south of the country.
In a post on X, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced the "interception and destruction of 3 drones in the Riyadh region and the southern region."
He did not specify where the drones came from, but the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's involvement in the Yemen war.
Earlier Monday, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at Riyadh. The Saudis have on the kingdom's infrastructure.
Source tells CBS News why report of rift between Netanyahu and his army chief over Iran seems credible
Israeli TV station Channel 12 reported Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had fallen out with army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive on Iran.
Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have both denied the reports, but a senior Israeli source with deep knowledge of the people involved has told CBS News the report of a rift seems credible.

The biggest tell, the source said, is that the Channel 12 report passed through military censorship. All stories by Israeli media that deal with national security must go through the censor before publication. This is key, according to the source, because it indicates that military brass felt it was necessary for the public to have the information before Israeli parliamentary elections on Tuesday.
Had it been false, the military censor would have simply prevented it from being published, the source told CBS News.

The other sign the report may be true is that Zamir, according to the source, is not personally opposed to renewed attacks on Iran – he's just opposed to the timing. The source said while there are likely new threats emerging from Iran, the question for commanders is whether new strikes need to happen now.
The military appears to believe that nothing requires a response within such a short timeframe, as Israelis prepare to cast their votes, according to the source.
Iranian president says insecurity created by the U.S. is harmful to the entire world

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that insecurity created by the United States in the Middle East was harming the entire world, as he prepared to travel to Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) at the invitation of Russia's president Vladimir Putin.

Pezeshkian said the GECF has 12 member countries and, together with its eight observer members, oversees more than 70% of the world's gas supply. He added that a substantial share of the energy needed globally is exported by these nations.

"The problems the United States has created by igniting war in the region and bringing insecurity to Europe have disrupted the free flow of energy," Pezeshkian said, apparently referring to the ongoing U.S.-Iran war and Putin's long-standing claim that the U.S. and Europe are responsible for .
He said his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity.
Egyptian parliament gives president authority to send troops to Saudi Arabia

Egypt's parliament on Monday approved a request by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that allows him to send troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Egypt's House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported.
El-Sisi that it would only be a defensive mission, "and does not include an attack on Yemen."
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.

Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of the recent military conflicts across the Middle East and has been involved in some mediation efforts. Some in the country view that as one of el-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But political analyst Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier, told CBS News it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments to help secure the region.
"This is a time of war, not politics and statements," he said last week. "If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
Saudi-led coalition claims to have destroyed Houthi missile tunnels and launchers

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Monday that its forces carried out a military operation targeting areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in response to repeated attacks by the group using ballistic missiles and drones.
In a statement posted on X, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said the operation sought to neutralize "the sources of threat," and included strikes against Houthi military infrastructure.
"The operation included the destruction of (5) tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, (4) ballistic missile launchers, and a missile storage [unit]," Al-Malki said.
He added that the operation sought to disrupt supply lines between areas under Houthi control, targeting "fortifications, elements, and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen."

Al-Malki said the operation was conducted in response to repeated Houthi attacks allegedly targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. He said the coalition would continue taking "deterrent operational measures" to protect Saudi and Yemeni civilians.
He said the operation was conducted "in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law."
Earlier, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
Iran's foreign minister praises Iran's resilience

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has praised his nation's resilience after nearly eight months of war with the U.S., crediting civil defense efforts, national mobilization and cooperation between the armed forces and diplomatic service.

"The victorious resistance of our beloved country during the enemy's two recent acts of aggression has been made possible only through the solidarity and mobilization of all military and civilian sectors, as well as the proud presence of all segments of the Iranian people on the front lines of resistance," he said in a message marking Iran's Civil Defense Week.
Araghchi added that close coordination between the armed forces and the diplomatic service had brought "great achievements" in safeguarding Iran's independence and dignity.
He said the foreign ministry would use its diplomatic capabilities to defend the country politically and legally and protect national interests.
"It will spare no effort in pursuing this mission," Araghchi said.

Last week, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal that the shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, had run dry.

The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries.
The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command.
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10%, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.
Tanker struck Friday in the Strait of Hormuz, maritime monitor says
A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Monday.
The maritime monitor said it received a "verified time-late report" of the incident, in which "a tanker transiting outbound was struck by an unknown projectile, disabling the vessel."
In a post on X, UKMTO said "the crew have been reported safe."

Iran claimed to have struck at least four tankers near the strait on Thursday last week, but there was no corroboration of its claims, and President Trump accused the Iranian regime of inventing attacks on commercial vessels in a bid to hike up global oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Israel defense chief denies report of rift between Netanyahu and army chief over Iran

Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday rejected reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders - most notably Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - over the prospect of new strikes in the war with Iran as "entirely baseless."
Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive.

Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterized it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu administration's judgement on the eve of close parliamentary elections that could unseat him.

"The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF [army] on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X, insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two.

In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received. The outlet did not offer details of the purported directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain.
CBS/AFP
Brent crude oil hovers around $115 a barrel after small drop

The price of Brent crude oil hovered around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging at the end of last week over global supply concerns linked to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as the northern hemisphere heads into the gas-hungry winter.
President Trump has fueled speculation that he could order a resumption of U.S. strikes on Iran after next Tuesday's midterm elections.
The president told Fox News on Sunday: "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all."

Additional U.S. forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, have been sent to the region, though U.S. diplomatic staffing levels have been reduced, and sources told CBS News last week that the overall American military footprint in the Middle East was also .
CBS/AFP
Iran says outcome of Israeli elections "makes no difference"
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference".

"It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls.
Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israel had "intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections."
CBS/AFP
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to hold talks with Iran Monday in Tehran, officials say
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said.
The meeting will follow eight months of war in the Middle East and recent U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran.

"As agreed, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defense minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday.
"The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X.
It is aimed at "promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan," he added.
Conflicting claims after Houthis say they attacked airport in Saudi capital hours after it reopened

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting alongside the Yemeni government in the country's civil war said Monday it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh.
A Houthi spokesperson, just hours after it resumed flights. Deadly strikes by the rebel group earlier this month had forced the airport to shut down operations for more than two weeks .

Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday that air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's capital Sanaa.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group "successfully targeted" the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones.
Saree previously warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target," as the airport prepared to resume international flights.
The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom's flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down over the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war that erupted in February.
CBS/AFP
Netanyahu warns Iran may use attacks to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts.
"The IDF is prepared in both defense and offense," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday, using the acronym for the Israeli army.

"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," he added. "Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows."
CBS/AFP
Trump says he's weighing deal with Iran against action to "finish them off"

President Trump said Sunday morning that he's deciding between reaching an agreement with Tehran and taking action to "finish them off," after suggesting Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," in reference to the U.S. and Israel's joint military campaign against Iran.
"Now, my question is, do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?" said Mr. Trump in an interview with Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures."

He also claimed that the U.S. now controls the Strait of Hormuz and criticized former President Barack Obama for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, which is better known as the Iran nuclear deal. Obama signed the agreement in 2015, but Mr. Trump pulled out of it during his first term in office.
Iran says potential new U.S. strikes wouldn't change its position
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks came amid mounting tensions between Tehran and Washington after President Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on Feb. 28.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."

Direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have appeared to stall for weeks, but Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said earlier Sunday that Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and messages were still being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries.
CBS/AFP
